paras: The attempted lynching of Charles Smith took place on the night of November 13, 1903, in Washington, D.C., when a crowd that had chased Smith, a Black youth accused of robbing a cafe cashier and shooting two policemen, beat him and shouted for his lynching as he was captured in an alley off New York Avenue. Police held the crowd back until a patrol wagon arrived, and Smith was held for the grand jury. Out-of-town papers stressed that it happened within sight of the White House, and one wire version said a "race riot" had barely been averted.

Smith, described as an 18- or 19-year-old "colored boy" or "negro," had been a dishwasher at the Treasury Cafe on G Street until his discharge a few days earlier, and knew that the cashier, Philip E. Steuart, closed up alone with the day's receipts.

At about 8:30 that evening a man masked with a cafe napkin held up Steuart with a revolver and took $28. Steuart gave chase blowing a police whistle, and crossing policemen and a growing number of pedestrians joined him. Crossing Policeman George W. Osburn was shot in the leg, and at the mouth of an alley behind the Oxford Hotel a bullet struck Crossing Policeman Channing M. Edwards over the heart but only grazed the skin. Edwards then overpowered and disarmed Smith.

The Star reported shouts of "Kill him" and "Lynch him" and said some uniformed policemen "took part in the rough handling of the prisoner." In the Times's account, three more officers arrived just ahead of the "infuriated crowd" and protected Smith "only by a stiff fight" until the wagon came. A wire report printed in St. Louis said several hundred people rushed Smith, answering police pleas with "Give him to us and we will finish him!", while another wire version said police clubbed him and citizens joined the beating. Smith reached the first precinct station with "a few cuts and bruises."

The next morning Smith told the Times that a white man named Tommy Brown had given him the pistol and threatened him into the robbery. Judge Scott of the Police Court held him for the grand jury on charges of highway robbery and assault with intent to kill, and later added $1,000 bond on a housebreaking charge. No later report of a trial was found, nor any arrest or inquiry concerning the crowd or the police beating.

Officials honored the wounded officers instead: Commissioner Macfarland visited Osburn, Edwards was offered a place on the regular force, and citizens planned a benefit for Osburn, whose shortened leg ended his police service.

The Washington papers treated the episode as a crime story, the Star under "Held Up a Cashier" with "Threats of Lynching Made" as a subhead and the Times under "Policemen Shot Down by Negro Highwayman." The Times dwelt on the officers' bravery, while the Star said police had joined in roughing up the prisoner.

Wire reports led with the lynching threat instead: the St. Louis Republic headlined "Tried to Lynch Negro in Front of White House," and the Marshalltown, Iowa, Evening Times-Republican "Negro Narrowly Escapes Lynching Within Sight of White House." The Marshalltown text called Smith a "negro desperado" and said the capital had been "in grave danger of being disgraced by a lynching and a race riot," yet added there was "no organized effort" to lynch him. The same text ran a week later in the Hot Springs (S.D.) Weekly Star as "Whites Threaten to Lynch a Negro Robber."

In Mississippi the Hattiesburg Daily Progress claimed "the army" had been needed to keep back the lynching, proof that presidents have "no weight when the common people feel that their quarrel is just." All of this coverage came from white papers; no Black-press report of the episode was found.

Crowd estimates range from "several hundred" to 500. Only the Marshalltown wire version reported that Black onlookers protested Smith's treatment, were beaten, and left when outnumbered by whites; neither Washington paper mentions this. The Star said Smith answered not guilty, while the Times first said he pleaded guilty before reporting not guilty the next day.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Charles Smith
bases: A crowd that had joined the chase shouted 'Lynch him' and rushed or beat Smith, a Black youth just captured on robbery and shooting accusations, and police kept him from it (A1, A2, A3, A5).

A crowd of several hundred (A2) or 500 (A5) acting on the robbery and shooting accusation demanded Smith's lynching and beat him, but police held it back and he was jailed alive (A1, A3); no one was killed, so this was an attempted lynching, not a lynching.
Two Washington papers (A1, A3) and two differently worded wire versions (A2, A5) agree on the robbery, the shootings, the cries to lynch Smith and the police holding the crowd back.

accounts.label: Evening Star (local)
accounts.gist: The crowd shouted 'Kill him' and 'Lynch him'; some uniformed police took part in rough handling, but police surrounded Smith and kept the crowd back; he had a few cuts and bruises.

accounts.label: Washington Times (local)
accounts.gist: Edwards captured Smith after a fierce struggle; three more officers arrived just ahead of the 'infuriated crowd' and protected him by a 'stiff fight' until the patrol wagon came.

accounts.label: Wire report (St. Louis Republic)
accounts.gist: Several hundred people rushed Smith as police tried to bring him out of the alley; police held him there until reinforced and the crowd was forced back.

accounts.label: Wire report (Marshalltown, Hot Springs)
accounts.gist: A mob of 500 beat Smith and demanded his lynching; police clubbed him while disarming him; Black onlookers who protested were beaten and fights followed; there was 'no organized effort' to lynch him.

accounts.label: Smith's own story
accounts.gist: Smith said a white man named Tommy Brown showed him the pistol, proposed the robbery for $10 and threatened him when he hesitated.

accounts.label: Hattiesburg editorial
accounts.gist: The whole police force and the army camped in Washington were needed to keep back the lynching.

framing.detail: The Evening Star headlined 'Held Up a Cashier' with 'Threats of Lynching Made' as a subhead, and stated that some police took part in the rough handling.
The Washington Times ran 'Policemen Shot Down by Negro Highwayman' and 'Police Probe Record of Bold Highwayman', praising the officers' fight to protect the prisoner.
The St. Louis Republic headlined 'Tried to Lynch Negro in Front of White House'.
The Marshalltown wire text called Smith a 'negro desperado' and said the capital was in 'grave danger of being disgraced by a lynching and a race riot'.
The Hattiesburg Daily Progress said the near-lynching showed presidents have 'no weight when the common people feel that their quarrel is just'.

Two policemen shot (Osburn seriously, Edwards slightly); the papers do not state their race
A crowd of several hundred to 500 pursuers and onlookers, mostly white per the wire; some police joined the beating
Pursuit, beating, threats and a rush on the prisoner; 'siege' overstates police holding Smith in an alley for minutes until the wagon came

info: Night of Friday, November 13, 1903, about 8:20-8:30 p.m.
Treasury Cafe, G Street near 14th/15th Streets NW, and an alley on the north side of New York Avenue behind the Oxford Hotel, near the Treasury Department and the White House
Charles Smith, described as a 'colored boy' or 'negro', aged 18 or 19, a recently discharged dishwasher at the cafe

Accused of robbing cashier Philip E. Steuart of $28 at gunpoint and of shooting Crossing Policemen Osburn and Edwards; later also charged with housebreaking (breaking The Hub's show window on October 26)
A crowd of pursuing pedestrians and citizens; some uniformed police also took part in the rough handling (Star) or clubbed Smith while disarming him (wire)
Smith was protected by police, taken to the first precinct station, arraigned before Judge Scott the next morning and committed to jail

sources.note: Fullest local account: robbery, chase, shootings, cries of 'Kill him' and 'Lynch him', police part in rough handling, arraignment before Judge Scott.

The excited crowd would undoubtedly have done him serious harm had not the police surrounded the prisoner and kept the crowd back.
